chapter_title: Introduction to Animation in Maya & Keyframe Animation
chapter_summary:
Animation is the art of bringing static objects to life, creating the illusion of movement over time. In Autodesk Maya, animation is fundamentally built upon the concept of keyframes. A keyframe is a recorded state of an object's attribute (like its position, rotation, or scale) at a specific point in time. When you set multiple keyframes for an object at different times, Maya interpolates, or calculates, the intermediate frames between those keyframes, creating a smooth transition from one state to the next. This is the core principle behind all animation in Maya, from a simple bouncing ball to complex character performances.

To begin animating in Maya, you'll primarily interact with the **Time Slider**, located at the bottom of the Maya interface. This horizontal bar represents the duration of your animation, typically measured in frames. Below the Time Slider, the **Range Slider** allows you to define the playback range (the portion of the animation that will be played) and the overall animation length. Understanding these two components is crucial for managing your animation sequences. You can adjust the current time by dragging the red vertical line (the Current Time Indicator) along the Time Slider, or by entering a specific frame number in the Current Time field.

Setting a keyframe is a straightforward process. First, select the object you wish to animate. Then, move the Current Time Indicator to the desired frame. Next, either press the 's' key on your keyboard (which sets a keyframe for all animatable attributes of the selected object) or right-click on specific attributes in the Channel Box (e.g., Translate X, Rotate Y, Scale Z) and choose "Key Selected." When an attribute has a keyframe set, its corresponding field in the Channel Box will turn red, and a red tick mark will appear on the Time Slider at that frame. To create motion, you'll advance the time, modify the object's attributes (e.g., move it, rotate it), and then set another keyframe. Maya will then generate the in-between frames.

A powerful feature for accelerating your animation workflow is **Auto Keyframe**. When enabled (by clicking the small key icon with a red circle in the Time Slider controls), Maya automatically sets a keyframe for any attribute you modify *if* that attribute already has a keyframe at the current time. If it doesn't have a keyframe, it will create one. This means you can simply move your object, change its rotation, or scale it at different frames, and Maya will automatically record those changes as keyframes. While convenient, it's a common mistake for beginners to leave Auto Keyframe on accidentally, leading to unintended keyframes and animation changes. Always be mindful of its status and toggle it off when you're just adjusting an object's position for modeling or scene setup, not for animation.

Controlling the playback speed and frame rate is another important aspect. In game development, animation is often targeted for specific frame rates, commonly 30 or 60 frames per second (fps). You can configure Maya's playback settings by navigating to **Window > Settings/Preferences > Preferences**, then selecting the "Time Slider" category. Here, you can set the "Playback speed" to "Real-time (24 fps)" or "Play every frame, Max Real-time" depending on your needs. For game animation, "Play every frame, Max Real-time" is often preferred during blocking stages to ensure every frame is evaluated, even if it means playback is slower than real-time on complex scenes. However, for final review, "Real-time" is essential to judge the timing accurately.

When reviewing your animation, you'll often use **Playblast**. A Playblast generates a quick, hardware-rendered preview of your animation, saving it as a video file (e.g., .mov, .avi). This is significantly faster than a full software render and provides an accurate representation of your animation's timing and motion. To create a Playblast, go to **Window > Playblast > Playblast Options** (the small square next to the menu item). Here, you can specify the output format, resolution, scale, and whether to save it to a file. Always use Playblast to review your work; relying solely on the in-viewport playback can be misleading due to potential frame drops on complex scenes.

Finally, managing your keyframes is just as important as setting them. You can select keyframes on the Time Slider by clicking them, or by dragging a box around multiple keyframes. Once selected, you can move them (drag-and-drop), scale them (using the Shift + drag on the ends of the selection), or delete them (press Delete). Accidental deletion or misplacement of keyframes is a common beginner error that can break your animation. Always observe the Time Slider and Channel Box carefully when making changes. By mastering these fundamental keyframing techniques, you lay the essential groundwork for creating dynamic and expressive animations in Maya.

screens.title: Introduction to Keyframe Animation in Maya
screens.subtitle: Bring objects to life using keyframes, the Time Slider, and fast preview workflows

narration.text: Animation turns still models into motion by saving snapshots of an object’s attributes over time. In Maya that snapshot is a keyframe: a recorded state for a property like position, rotation, or scale at a specific frame. In this lesson you will learn the core interface elements — the Time Slider for moving through frames, the Range Slider for defining playback windows, and the Channel Box where attributes turn red when keyed. You will practice setting keys manually, use Auto Keyframe to speed repetitive work, and learn how to avoid the common mistake of leaving Auto Key on and accidentally recording motion. We’ll also cover playback settings so your timing matches the target frame rate and Playblast to produce quick viewport previews without a full render. By the end you will be able to create simple motion, edit timing directly on the Time Slider, and produce a fast, accurate preview for review. Think of keyframing as plotting important moments; the rest of animation is deciding how those moments relate in time.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Keyframes mark important states. Maya interpolates between keys to create motion; the Time and Range Sliders plus the Channel Box are your primary tools for controlling and inspecting that motion.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter — practical, verifiable skills

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will reliably find and use Maya’s core animation controls, set and inspect keyframes, and manage timing for expressive motion. First, you will identify the Time Slider and Range Slider and explain how they define current time and playback windows. Second, you will be able to state what a keyframe records and why interpolation between keys creates motion. Third, you will practice setting, editing, and deleting keyframes for position, rotation, and scale using both the general set key command and the Channel Box’s Key Selected. Finally, you will enable and disable Auto Keyframe intentionally, understanding when it speeds your work and when it creates accidental keys. Each objective includes a competency milestone you can verify by demonstrating the action in a scene. These skills ensure you can block out motion, refine timing, and produce quick previews for review, which are essential steps in both film and game pipelines.

screens.title: Time Slider and Range Slider
screens.subtitle: Control current time, playback range, and overall animation length

narration.text: The Time Slider is the backbone of Maya animation. It shows frames horizontally and lets you set the Current Time by dragging the red Current Time Indicator or by entering a frame number. The Range Slider sits just below it and defines which portion of the timeline is visible and plays back; you can use its handles to focus on a subset of frames while you refine motion. Together they let you scrub to a frame, block animation segments, and test short sections quickly. For an example, imagine animating a 48-frame walk cycle: set your overall scene length to 48 frames, then shrink the Range Slider to test frames 1–24 when polishing the contact-to-passing poses. A common misconception is that changing the Range Slider edits keyframes — it only adjusts visibility and the playback window; keys remain at their absolute frames. Practical tips: set the Current Time field to jump precisely to a frame, use the Range Slider to loop a segment while you refine, and ensure your scene playback range matches your intended loop or shot length. Why does this matter? Precise control of time simplifies timing adjustments and speeds iteration when you only need to tweak a few frames.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Time and Range Sliders let you navigate and focus your attention on specific frames, enabling precise timing changes without altering key placement.

screens.title: What is a Keyframe?
screens.subtitle: A saved attribute state at a specific frame that defines an important moment in motion

narration.text: A keyframe is a recorded state of one or more attributes of an object at a particular frame. Think of it as a photograph capturing position, rotation, and scale at a moment in time. When Maya finds two or more keyframes on an attribute, it interpolates the values between them to create the in-between frames that you see as motion. For example, if Translate X is keyed at 0 on frame 1 and at 5 on frame 24, Maya calculates intermediate Translate X values for frames 2 through 23 to produce a smooth transition. This raises a common misconception: keys do not store motion, they store discrete values; motion is the result of interpolation between those stored values. Another important point is that different attributes can be keyed independently — you might key position at three frames and rotation at others. This gives you control to stagger timing across attributes for more natural motion. A quick practical check is to move an object and set keys at separate frames; then scrub the Time Slider and observe how the Channel Box values update according to interpolation. What attribute will you key first when planning a shot?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Keyframes store attribute values at frames; interpolation makes the motion between keys.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is a Keyframe?
Concept
A keyframe records the value of an attribute at a particular frame. Interpolation creates the motion between keyed values.
Stores attribute values like Translate X, Rotate Y, or Scale Z.
Interpolation fills frames between keys to form continuous motion.
Attributes can be keyed independently to stagger timing.
Key Takeaway

Keys are snapshots; the feel of motion depends on where you place those snapshots in time.

Example
Key Translate X at frame 1 to 0 and at frame 24 to 5. Scrub the timeline and notice how the value changes smoothly due to interpolation.
Common misconception
Keys do not contain an animation curve by themselves; they are points on a curve Maya constructs. Removing keys removes the points that define motion.
Check your understanding
If you move an object at frame 10 but do not set a key, will the motion be recorded? No — without a key, Maya has no saved value at that frame and will not interpolate from that change.

screens.title: Setting, Editing, and Deleting Keyframes
screens.subtitle: Practical steps to record and refine attribute keys using 's' and Channel Box operations

narration.text: Setting a keyframe is a simple sequence but precise timing and attribute selection are critical. Start by selecting the object you want to animate and move the Current Time Indicator to the desired frame. Press the 's' key to set keys for all animatable attributes, or right-click a specific attribute name in the Channel Box and choose Key Selected to record only that attribute. When a key is set, the Channel Box field turns red and a red tick appears on the Time Slider. To edit keys, select the key markers on the Time Slider and drag them left or right to change timing. To scale motion, select a range of keys and shift-drag the ends to compress or expand timing proportionally. To delete a key, select it and press Delete. A common beginner mistake is moving objects and assuming a key exists; always confirm the red indicators. Another frequent error is deleting keys accidentally — when deleting, watch the Channel Box and Time Slider for removed markers. Practice by keying Translate X on frames 1, 24, and 48 and then moving the middle key closer to speed up the middle action.

keyIdea.title: Practical sequence
keyIdea.text: Use 's' for all attributes, Key Selected for fine control, and the Time Slider to move, scale, or delete keys for timing edits.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Set / Edit / Delete Keys
Process Flow
Quick workflow
  1. Select object and move Current Time Indicator to the frame.
  2. Press s to key all animatable attributes.
  3. Or right-click an attribute in the Channel Box and choose Key Selected.
  4. Confirm the Channel Box field turns red and a red tick appears on the Time Slider.
Editing keys
  • Drag key ticks to move timing.
  • Select keys and Shift-drag ends to scale a selection.
  • Select a key and press Delete to remove it.
Example exercise
Key Translate X at frames 1, 24, and 48. Then select the frame 24 key and drag it left to make the movement happen earlier and appear faster. Observe Channel Box values as you scrub.
Common mistake

Forgetting to check the Channel Box after moving an object will leave you thinking a key exists when it doesn't. Always confirm the red indicators.

Key Takeaway

Precise key placement and verification prevent timing errors and accidental edits.

screens.title: Auto Keyframe vs Manual Keying
screens.subtitle: When to let Maya record changes automatically and when to key intentionally

narration.text: Auto Keyframe is a convenience that saves time by recording changes automatically as you modify attributes. When Auto Key is enabled, any attribute you change at the current frame will become keyed — if no key existed at that frame Maya creates one. This can dramatically speed blocking passes where you make many sequential changes. However, a common beginner error is leaving Auto Key on during scene setup or modeling, which creates unintended keys and breaks animations later. Manual keying — using the 's' hotkey or Key Selected — is slower but deliberate: you only key attributes you intend to animate. To decide which to use, ask whether you are experimenting quickly or making deliberate animation decisions. For example, in blocking you might enable Auto Key to try poses rapidly. Later, when polishing or modeling, turn Auto Key off and set keys intentionally. A useful workflow is to enable Auto Key for short bursts and double-check the Time Slider for unexpected red ticks when you finish. Which mode will you use when first blocking a motion and why? Auto Keyframe vs Manual Keying means auto keyframe speeds recording but can create accidental keys; manual keying offers precise control when refining or modeling.. In practical terms, when to let maya record changes automatically and when to key intentionally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choice
keyIdea.text: Auto Keyframe speeds recording but can create accidental keys; manual keying offers precise control when refining or modeling.

Comparison
Auto Keyframe
Automatically creates keys when you change attributes. Fast during blocking but risky during modeling.
Speed: High
Control: Lower
Risk: Accidental keys if left on
Pro tip

Enable Auto Key for early blocking, then disable it before modeling or detailed edits to prevent unwanted key creation.

Manual Keying
Use 's' or Key Selected to record keys intentionally. Slower but precise, essential for polishing and final timing work.
Speed: Moderate
Control: High
Safety: Safer for long scenes
Key Takeaway

Use Auto Key for rapid blocking; switch to manual keying for refinement to avoid accidental keys.

screens.title: Channel Box and Attribute Indicators
screens.subtitle: How Maya displays keyed attributes and how to interpret the visual cues

narration.text: The Channel Box provides immediate feedback about which attributes are animated. When an attribute has a keyframe at the current frame, Maya colors the attribute field red. This visual cue is essential: it confirms that a value will be recorded during playback and that editing the value affects animation. On the Time Slider you will also see a red tick that denotes the keyed frame for the object. Together these signals help you avoid the common confusion of moving geometry without recording a key. For example, if Translate Y is red at frame 24, changing its value will update the animation curve unless you deliberately remove the key. Another helpful detail is that attributes can have keys on some frames and not others; an attribute might be keyed only at frames 1 and 48, leaving the middle frames to interpolation. A practical habit is to glance at the Channel Box after making a transform to confirm the red highlight. If you see unexpected red attributes, check whether Auto Key was on. This simple inspection step prevents many unintended animation errors.

keyIdea.title: Visual feedback
keyIdea.text: Red attribute text and red ticks on the Time Slider show where keys exist; use them to confirm your intended edits are recorded.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Channel Box Indicators
Architecture
Key visual cues
  • Channel Box attribute field turns red when keyed at the current frame.
  • Time Slider shows a red tick at frames with keys for the selected object.
  • Attributes can be keyed independently, creating staggered timing across properties.
Example

Set Translate X at frame 1 and Translate Y at frame 12. You will see red in the Channel Box only for the attributed keyed at the current frame when you scrub.

Quick checks
After moving geometry, confirm the Channel Box color and Time Slider ticks. If you find unexpected red fields, Auto Key may have created keys unintentionally.
Misconception: Red means locked — actually it means keyed for that frame.
Pro tip: Use Key Selected to avoid turning multiple attributes red when you only intend to change one.
Key Takeaway

Channel Box color and Time Slider ticks are your immediate confirmation tools for keyed attributes.

screens.title: Playback Speed and Frame Rate
screens.subtitle: Configure playback behavior to match your target frame rate and timing needs

narration.text: Accurate playback is essential to judge timing. Maya provides playback settings in Preferences under the Time Slider category where you set playback speed modes such as Real-time or Play every frame. For game targets you will often pick 30 or 60 frames per second, while film work might use 24. Real-time playback attempts to match the selected fps, skipping frames on heavy scenes, while Play every frame ensures every frame is evaluated, even if it plays slower than real-time. During blocking you may prefer Play every frame so every key and expression is calculated for correct spacing and timing, even at the cost of performance. For final timing checks use Real-time to evaluate whether the motion feels correct at the intended frame rate. A misconception is thinking playback choice rewrites timing; it does not change key locations — it only affects how frames are evaluated and displayed. Always confirm your Preferences playback mode before judging speed and make Playblast videos for definitive timing checks. Playback Speed and Frame Rate means playback mode affects evaluation fidelity: choose play every frame for accurate calculation, real-time to judge final feel at a target fps.. In practical terms, configure playback behavior to match your target frame rate and timing needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Playback accuracy
keyIdea.text: Playback mode affects evaluation fidelity: choose Play every frame for accurate calculation, Real-time to judge final feel at a target fps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Playback & Frame Rate
Process
Playback modes
Real-time Attempts to play at the selected fps; may skip frames on heavy scenes.
Play every frame Evaluates every frame even if playback is slower than real-time — useful for blocking.
Example
If you target a 24 fps film shot, use Real-time for final feel. For checking curve evaluation, use Play every frame to ensure each key and expression is calculated.
How to set
  1. Open Window > Settings/Preferences > Preferences.
  2. Select Time Slider and choose the desired playback speed and fps.
  3. Test both modes to see which reveals timing issues for your scene complexity.
Key Takeaway

Playback mode affects evaluation and perception of timing; choose according to the review stage.

screens.title: Playblast — Fast Previewing
screens.subtitle: Create quick, hardware-rendered previews to check timing without a full render

narration.text: Playblast produces a viewport-based video that reflects the timing and motion of your scene without running a full render. It uses the G P U to capture frames quickly and saves them as a video file you can share or scrub. To create a Playblast, choose Window, Playblast and open Playblast Options. There you set output format, resolution, scale, and whether to save a file. Use Playblast when you need a reliable view of timing across machines or to send a quick preview to a teammate. A common pitfall is relying only on in-viewport playback, which can drop frames on heavy scenes and misrepresent timing. Playblast removes that ambiguity by capturing rendered frames into a file. For example, make a short Playblast of a 48-frame animation to verify timing on another machine or to proof an animation loop. Keep Playblast resolution modest for speed, and use a higher resolution only when you need a closer look at motion details. Playblast — Fast Previewing means playblast saves a viewport-rendered video for accurate timing checks faster than a full render.. In practical terms, create quick, hardware-rendered previews to check timing without a full render. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Playblast saves a viewport-rendered video for accurate timing checks faster than a full render.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Playblast
Definition
Why Playblast
Fast, hardware-rendered preview that captures timing reliably.
Useful for reviews, sharing with teammates, and diagnosing timing differences across machines.
Workflow
  1. Open Window > Playblast > Playblast Options.
  2. Choose format, set resolution/scale, and select save location if needed.
  3. Generate the Playblast and review the resulting video for timing accuracy.
Example
Create a Playblast for a 48-frame run. Use a lower resolution for speed while reviewing motion and increase only when detail inspection is needed.
Common mistake

Relying on viewport playback alone can hide dropped frames; Playblast provides a recorded representation of timing for dependable review.

Key Takeaway

Always produce Playblasts for final timing checks and when sharing work for review.

screens.title: Animating a Simple Box Movement — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Create a cube and set three key poses to form a basic motion arc

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on exercise step by step so you can practice the core keyframing skills. Start a new scene and create a polygon cube. Set the Time Slider to frame 1 and select the cube. In the Channel Box, right-click Translate X, Translate Y, and Translate Z and choose Key Selected; you'll see red ticks appear on frame 1 and the attribute fields turn red. Next, move the Current Time Indicator to frame 24 and use the Move tool to reposition the cube to a new pose, for example Translate X = 5, Translate Y = 2. Key the three translate channels again. Finally, go to frame 48 and move the cube to a third pose such as Translate X = -5, Translate Y = 0, and key once more. Scrub the Time Slider to see the cube travel through those three poses. This exercise reinforces setting keys for specific attributes and observing the interpolation Maya creates between them. A common oversight is failing to confirm the Channel Box colors, so pause and verify that each keyed attribute turned red after keying.

keyIdea.title: Practice steps
keyIdea.text: Create a cube and set Translate keys at frames 1, 24, and 48; scrub to confirm interpolation creates motion between poses.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Box Movement — Part 1
Timeline
Step-by-step
  1. Create > Polygon Primitives > Cube.
  2. Set Time Slider to frame 1; Key Selected for Translate X,Y,Z.
  3. Move to frame 24; reposition cube to a second pose and key Translate channels.
  4. Move to frame 48; set a third pose and key again. Scrub to review the motion.
Example values
Frame 1: Translate X=0, Y=0. Frame 24: Translate X=5, Y=2. Frame 48: Translate X=-5, Y=0. These values create a clear arc and let you observe interpolation.
Common oversight

Not checking the Channel Box after setting keys can leave you unsure whether the key was recorded. Look for red attributes and ticks.

Key Takeaway

Practicing manual keying builds muscle memory for intentional timing adjustments.

screens.title: Animating a Simple Box Movement — Part 2 (Refine & Timing)
screens.subtitle: Edit key timing, scale key ranges, and create a Playblast for review

narration.text: Now that the cube moves between three keyed poses, refine timing and prepare a Playblast to evaluate the motion. First, select the middle key on the Time Slider and drag it left or right to speed up or slow down the middle action. To compress the whole motion, select all three keys and Shift-drag an end of the selection to scale the timing proportionally. Observe how changing key spacing alters the interpolation and the perceived weight of the motion. Once satisfied, configure playback settings if needed, then produce a Playblast via Window, Playblast, and set a modest resolution. Review the Playblast to judge timing on a consistent playback and to share with collaborators. A typical misconception is thinking scaling keys changes attribute values — it only changes their frame positions. Keep a backup by duplicating keys or saving incremental scene versions before wide-ranging edits. Finally, ask yourself whether the motion now reads faster or slower and adjust key spacing until the timing communicates the intent. In practical terms, edit key timing, scale key ranges, and create a playblast for review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Refine timing

  • Select multiple keys and Shift-drag an end to scale the selection.
  • Observe how compression or expansion changes the perceived speed and weight.
Safety tip

Save an incremental scene or duplicate keys before large timing changes so you can revert if needed.

  2. Choose a low resolution for speed and set a save location if needed.
  3. Generate and review the video to confirm timing across machines.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common Keyframing Errors
screens.subtitle: Diagnose accidental keys, dropped frames, and unexpected interpolation

narration.text: As you learn keyframing, you will run into a few recurring errors. First, accidental keys from leaving Auto Key enabled — symptoms include unexpected red ticks on the Time Slider and red attribute fields in the Channel Box after unrelated edits. If this happens, undo the change or delete the unwanted keys and remember to toggle Auto Key off. Second, dropped frames in viewport playback can create the illusion of incorrect timing. Use Play every frame to evaluate curves precisely and generate a Playblast for a definitive check. Third, unexpected interpolation happens when you assume linear spacing but have eased tangents or different interpolation modes; inspect curves in the Graph Editor if motion feels wrong. Lastly, deleting keys unintentionally can break motion — confirm selection before pressing Delete and use incremental saves. A helpful diagnostic routine: check Auto Key status, confirm Channel Box colors, test playback with Play every frame, and make a Playblast. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Troubleshooting
Common Mistakes
Accidental Auto Key
If unexpected keys appear, disable Auto Key, remove the unwanted keys, and replay to confirm normal behavior.
Symptom
Red ticks appear after a modeling move.
Dropped frames vs real timing
Use Play every frame to evaluate every key and Playblast to produce a consistent playback file for judgment.
Unexpected interpolation
If motion eases unexpectedly, check tangent types in the Graph Editor; keys are points, tangents shape the curve between them.
Accidental deletion
Confirm selection before Delete and keep incremental saves. Restoring from an earlier save is faster than reconstructing complex timing.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep these three compact ideas in mind as you continue practicing. First, a keyframe records an attribute value at a specific frame; interpolation creates motion between keys. Second, Time Slider and Range Slider are your navigation and focus tools — they control current time and visible playback range but do not move keys. Third, Auto Keyframe speeds recording but can create accidental keys; use it deliberately and verify keys via the Channel Box and Time Slider. These three ideas will guide safe and efficient keyframing: record intentionally, inspect visual cues, and use Playblast for reliable timing checks. When in doubt, slow down, confirm red attribute indicators, and use manual keying for final adjustments. Which concept will you rehearse first in your next animation session? screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders to improve your keyframe workflow

narration.text: To finish, lock in these practical reminders: always confirm keys by checking Channel Box color and Time Slider ticks, use Auto Key for quick blocking but switch to manual keying for refinement, and rely on Playblast for consistent timing review. These routines will reduce accidental keys, help you make intentional timing choices, and provide dependable previews to share with teammates. Practicing the hands-on cube exercise and deliberately toggling Auto Key on and off will make these habits second nature. When you next animate, ask yourself: did I set the key, did I confirm the indicator, and did I produce a Playblast for review?
